subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In a sample of double-stranded DNA, 20% of the bases are adenine. The percentage of cytosine is:
questions.explain: By Chargaff's rule A=T=20%, so G+C=60%, and since G=C, cytosine is 30%.

questions.q: If the supply of CO2 to a chloroplast is suddenly cut off, what happens to the level of RuBP in the Calvin cycle initially?
options: It falls rapidly as it is used up
It rises because it is no longer being converted to GP
It stays constant
It is converted to triose phosphate
questions.explain: Without CO2, RuBP cannot be fixed to GP, so RuBP accumulates while GP falls.

questions.q: When an enzyme is immobilised by entrapment in alginate beads, the rate of reaction may be slightly lower than for free enzyme because:
options: no enzyme-substrate complexes can form
the enzyme denatures instantly
the substrate must diffuse into the bead to reach the active sites, slowing the reaction
the optimum temperature falls to 0 C
questions.explain: Entrapment can hinder substrate access as it must diffuse through the matrix, though immobilisation still allows reuse and greater stability.

questions.q: In a commercial greenhouse, why might a grower add a carbon dioxide generator alongside extra lighting?
options: To prevent CO2 from becoming the limiting factor when light is plentiful
To stop the Calvin cycle
To denature plant enzymes
To reduce the rate of photosynthesis
questions.explain: With abundant light, raising CO2 stops it from limiting photosynthesis, allowing a higher overall rate.

questions.q: Cholesterol contributes to membrane stability at low temperatures by:
options: forming hydrophilic channels
allowing phospholipids to pack tightly and freeze solid
preventing the phospholipids from packing too closely, so the membrane does not become too rigid and stays fluid
increasing active transport
questions.explain: At low temperatures cholesterol stops phospholipids packing tightly together, maintaining fluidity and preventing the membrane becoming too rigid.

questions.q: Why is starch an effective storage molecule in plants but unsuitable as the main respiratory substrate transported in solution?
options: It cannot be hydrolysed to glucose
It is insoluble and compact so it does not affect water potential, but this also makes it unsuitable for transport
It is highly soluble and so leaks out of cells
It is too small to store energy
questions.explain: Starch's insolubility means it has no osmotic effect and stores compactly, but the same property makes it unsuitable for transport, where soluble sucrose is used instead.

questions.q: During the S phase of interphase, the key event is:
options: division of the cytoplasm
synthesis of spindle fibres only
separation of chromatids
semi-conservative replication of DNA so each chromosome consists of two identical sister chromatids
questions.explain: In the synthesis (S) phase DNA is replicated, producing two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere for each chromosome.

questions.q: The water potential of pure water at standard temperature and pressure is:
options: always negative
equal to the solute potential of the cell
a large positive value
zero
questions.explain: Pure water has the highest water potential, defined as 0 kPa; adding solute makes the water potential more negative.

questions.q: In telophase of mitosis:
options: chromosomes condense and the nuclear envelope breaks down
chromosomes line up at the equator
chromosomes decondense and two new nuclear envelopes form around the separated chromosomes
chromatids are pulled to opposite poles
questions.explain: Telophase sees the separated chromosomes reach the poles, decondense, and become enclosed by re-formed nuclear envelopes before cytokinesis.

questions.q: On a rate-against-substrate-concentration graph, increasing the concentration of a COMPETITIVE inhibitor would:
options: increase the substrate concentration needed to reach the same rate, but Vmax is still attainable
have no effect on the curve
prevent Vmax ever being reached even at infinite substrate
lower the Vmax that can be reached
questions.explain: Competitive inhibition can be overcome by sufficient substrate, so Vmax is unchanged but more substrate is needed to approach it.

questions.q: Why do lipids release more energy per gram than carbohydrates when respired?
options: They contain more carbon-hydrogen bonds to be oxidised, releasing more reduced coenzymes
They are more oxidised
They require no oxygen
They bypass the Krebs cycle
questions.explain: Lipids are highly reduced with many C-H bonds, so their oxidation yields more reduced NAD and FAD and thus more ATP.

questions.q: A plant cell becomes plasmolysed when placed in a concentrated salt solution because:
options: salt is actively pumped out of the cell
the cell wall ruptures
water enters the cell, pushing the membrane against the wall
water leaves the cell by osmosis, so the protoplast shrinks away from the cell wall
questions.explain: The external solution has a lower (more negative) water potential, so water leaves the cell and the plasma membrane pulls away from the wall.

questions.q: Which feature distinguishes RNA from DNA?
options: RNA nucleotides are joined by ester bonds, not phosphodiester bonds
RNA is double-stranded and helical
RNA contains thymine instead of uracil
RNA contains ribose and uracil
questions.explain: RNA uses the pentose ribose and the base uracil in place of thymine, and is typically single-stranded.

questions.q: Why does an enzyme show specificity for a particular substrate?
options: because the precise 3D shape of the active site, determined by tertiary structure, is complementary to one substrate
because the substrate has the same primary structure as the enzyme
because all enzymes catalyse every reaction
because the enzyme provides activation energy to all molecules equally
questions.explain: The active site's specific shape, arising from the protein's folding, is complementary only to a particular substrate, conferring specificity.

questions.q: Above the optimum temperature, enzyme activity falls because:
options: hydrogen and ionic bonds break, changing the tertiary structure and active site shape
the activation energy decreases too far
substrate molecules move too slowly to collide
more enzyme-substrate complexes form than can be processed
questions.explain: Excessive thermal energy breaks bonds holding the tertiary structure, denaturing the active site so the substrate no longer fits.

questions.q: Which molecule is phosphorylated using ATP at the start of glycolysis, before the sugar is split?
options: Pyruvate
Triose phosphate
Acetyl coenzyme A
Glucose (to glucose phosphate)
questions.explain: Glucose is first phosphorylated to glucose phosphate, making it more reactive before it is split into two triose phosphates.

questions.q: In the Krebs cycle, the regeneration of the 4-carbon acceptor molecule allows the cycle to:
options: Produce oxygen for the electron transport chain
Take place in the cytoplasm
Stop after one acetyl group is processed
Continuously accept further acetyl CoA molecules
questions.explain: Regenerating oxaloacetate means the cycle can keep accepting new acetyl groups, turning repeatedly as respiration continues.

questions.q: A channel protein differs from a carrier protein in facilitated diffusion in that a channel protein:
options: transports only non-polar molecules
uses ATP to move ions
changes shape to move molecules across
forms a hydrophilic pore allowing specific ions to pass without changing shape
questions.explain: Channel proteins provide a water-filled pore for specific ions to diffuse through, whereas carrier proteins change conformation to shuttle molecules across.

questions.q: Which feature of the chloroplast increases the surface area available for the light-dependent reactions?
options: The double outer envelope
The presence of starch grains
The stacked thylakoid membranes forming grana
The fluid-filled stroma
questions.explain: Thylakoids stacked into grana give a large membrane surface area for photosystems and electron carriers.

questions.q: Which statement about the role of reduced NAD and reduced FAD in respiration is correct?
options: They directly phosphorylate ADP to ATP
They are produced only during oxidative phosphorylation
They are the final electron acceptors of the chain
They deliver electrons and protons to the electron transport chain
questions.explain: Reduced coenzymes carry electrons and protons to the carriers on the inner membrane, feeding the chain.

questions.q: In one turn of the Krebs cycle, how many molecules of reduced NAD, reduced FAD and ATP are produced respectively?
options: 3 reduced NAD, 3 reduced FAD, 2 ATP
1 reduced NAD, 3 reduced FAD, 1 ATP
3 reduced NAD, 1 reduced FAD, 1 ATP
2 reduced NAD, 2 reduced FAD, 2 ATP
questions.explain: Each Krebs turn yields three reduced NAD, one reduced FAD and one ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation.

questions.q: Why is glycogen a more suitable storage molecule than cellulose in animal cells?
options: Its glycosidic bonds cannot be hydrolysed
It is unbranched and so packs tightly into fibres
It is highly branched, giving many free ends for rapid hydrolysis
It contains beta-glucose, which is more soluble
questions.explain: Glycogen's highly branched structure provides many terminal glucose units, allowing rapid enzymatic release of glucose to meet metabolic demand.

questions.q: A respiratory substrate gives a respiratory quotient (RQ) of about 0.7. Which substrate is most likely being respired?
options: Ethanol
Protein
Lipid
Carbohydrate
questions.explain: Lipids are highly reduced and require more oxygen relative to CO2 produced, giving an RQ around 0.7.

questions.q: Besides reduced NAD, what TWO products result from the link reaction per pyruvate molecule?
options: Acetyl coenzyme A and carbon dioxide
Glycerate-3-phosphate and oxygen
Lactate and ATP
Oxaloacetate and water
questions.explain: Each pyruvate is decarboxylated and combined with coenzyme A to form acetyl CoA, releasing CO2 and reducing NAD.

questions.q: End-product inhibition, a form of metabolic control, typically operates because the end product acts as a:
options: substrate for the first reaction
competitive inhibitor of the final enzyme
non-competitive (allosteric) inhibitor of an enzyme earlier in the pathway
coenzyme for the first enzyme
questions.explain: The end product binds allosterically to an early enzyme, reducing its activity and preventing wasteful overproduction; this is negative feedback.

questions.q: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) differs in function from RER in that the SER:
options: digests pathogens
synthesises and transports lipids and steroids and stores calcium ions
synthesises proteins
contains chlorophyll
questions.explain: The SER lacks ribosomes and is involved in lipid and steroid synthesis, plus calcium ion storage, rather than protein synthesis.

questions.q: Facilitated diffusion differs from simple diffusion in that it:
options: moves substances against their concentration gradient
uses channel or carrier proteins to move polar/charged molecules down their gradient
only occurs across the nuclear envelope
requires ATP
questions.explain: Facilitated diffusion is passive but uses transport proteins to allow polar or charged molecules to cross the hydrophobic bilayer, still down the gradient.

questions.q: In the condensation reaction forming a dipeptide, which statement is correct?
options: A peptide bond forms between an amine group and a carboxyl group with loss of water
A water molecule is added across the peptide bond
A glycosidic bond forms with release of water
A hydrogen bond forms between two R-groups
questions.explain: Condensation joins the amino group of one amino acid to the carboxyl group of another, forming a peptide bond and releasing water.

questions.q: How does anaerobic fermentation in yeast differ from that in mammalian muscle?
options: Yeast uses oxygen whereas muscle does not
Yeast produces ethanol and CO2; muscle produces lactate
Both produce ethanol but only muscle releases CO2
Yeast produces lactate; muscle produces ethanol
questions.explain: Yeast decarboxylates pyruvate and reduces it to ethanol, releasing CO2, whereas mammalian muscle forms lactate.

questions.q: A non-competitive inhibitor acts by:
options: being outcompeted by high substrate concentration
binding to an allosteric site away from the active site, altering the active site shape
increasing substrate affinity
binding to the active site and blocking substrate entry
questions.explain: Non-competitive inhibitors bind at a site other than the active site, changing the enzyme's tertiary structure so substrate can no longer bind effectively.
